results.title: Nebius Is Raising the Price of Its AI Compute on Oct. 1. Here's What That Says About the Shortage. | The Motley Fool
highlights:
## Key Points

- Nebius' on-demand hourly rates for four Nvidia GPU models climb between 17% and 21% on Oct. 1.
- Management says it could sell all its 2027 capacity today on the terms of its newest contracts.
- The company expects to spend $20 billion to $25 billion on capital expenditures this year.

Nebius Group (NBIS -9.92%) is about to charge more for the computing power it rents out by the hour. On Thursday, Oct. 1, the artificial intelligence (AI) cloud company's on-demand rate for an Nvidia B300 graphics processing unit (GPU) climbs 21%, from $7.85 per hour to $9.50.

Nebius expects to spend $20 billion to $25 billion on capital expenditures this year, versus guided revenue of $3 billion to $3.4 billion. A company building capacity so fast normally needs to work to fill it, not raise prices on it.

But what does a price hike now say about how tight AI computing supply is? I think it says plenty. Still, the increase itself touches a smaller share of Nebius' business than the new rates imply.

...

The Oct. 1 increase isn't the first this year. In early May, Nebius' pricing page showed the older H100 chip at $2.95 per hour and the B300 at $6.10.

After this round, the same chips will cost $4.50 and $9.50 -- around 53% and 56% more than five months before. This round includes four Nvidia GPUs (the H100, H200, B200, and B300), with hikes of 17% to 21%, plus Nebius' CPU-only servers.

What strikes me is the H100, a generation behind Nvidia's Blackwell chips (the B200 and B300). Rising prices for older hardware arguably say more about a shortage than a premium on the latest chip does. After all, Nebius' second-quarter shareholder letter already reported over 30% higher pricing for older-generation GPUs versus the first quarter.

...

"[W]e sold out of capacity because, as fast as we bring capacity online, we can sell it," CFO Dado Alonso said on the company's second-quarter earnings call in August.

CEO Arkady Volozh went further in the shareholder letter, saying Nebius could sell all its 2027 capacity today on the terms of its newest deals. It's saving some for customers with immediate needs instead. What's more, its first capacity auction cleared at the highest price Nebius has seen for Nvidia's Blackwell chips, 15% over anything it had charged earlier.

Its latest partnership tells the same story.

...

In short, I think the hike is what it looks like: a provider that can't add capacity as fast as customers want it.

...

The increase matters more as a benchmark for capacity Nebius hasn't sold yet. Showing how fast that price is rising, Nebius' annual contract value per megawatt went from a 2026 base of around $12 million to over $20 million on deals closed in the second quarter. Management also sees short-term deals at $40 million to $50 million per megawatt, and it signed the first one in the third quarter. And profitability has risen with those prices. The AI cloud business's non-GAAP (adjusted) margin on earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) almost doubled from the fourth quarter of 2025 to 45% in the first quarter. It widened again to around 50% in the second.

...

Of course, shortage pricing can reverse. If supply catches up to demand while Nebius and its rivals keep building, hourly rates might drop as fast as they rose. And the build-out is being funded partly by $5.75 billion in convertible notes sold in August and around $2.8 billion in new shares sold through June.

Ultimately, the Oct. 1 increase is strong evidence of how tight AI computing supply is right now. But it's a sign more than a revenue driver.

results.title: NVIDIA GPU Rental Prices Are Surging and Undercutting Michael Burry's Bear Case | DNA Compute Holdings LLC
highlights:
Kyle Reidhead argues that Michael Burry's bearish thesis on Nvidia - that GPUs become worthless after roughly three years while hyperscalers extend depreciation schedules to six - is being contradicted by rental market data.

He cites Nvidia GPU rental prices rising 30–58% this year across chip generations. The H100, now roughly three years old and two generations behind Nvidia's newest chips, is reportedly renting for about 40% more than it was in January.

He also notes that H100 prices did not decline after Blackwell-generation chips (B200, B300) rolled out at scale this year, which he argues would be expected if newer chips were making older ones obsolete.

The analysis suggests this trend could benefit neoclouds and hyperscalers that own large GPU fleets, since already-depreciated hardware would be generating rising rental income.

results.title: Nebius raises Nvidia GPU rental rates up to 21% effective October 1, led by B300 at $9.50/hr · AI Factor News
highlights:
A supplier raising prices into record capex is the strongest possible signal that AI compute demand still exceeds supply — including for last-gen H100s, up 53% since May. It is bullish for the entire AI infrastructure revenue chain (Nvidia's pricing power, Micron's memory pricing power, datacenter landlords), and it is pure pricing power for neoclouds. The bearish offset is real: it raises the cost floor for AI startups' unit economics, which is exactly why falling inference costs matter to the thesis — someone has to make the math work for the renters. For the overbuild debate, this is bear-case kryptonite in price form: overbuilt markets cut prices; this market raises them.

## Summary Nebius raised on-demand AI compute pricing 17-21% across H100/H200/B200/B300 effective October 1, with the B300 going from $7.85 to $9.50/hour — into a year when it is spending $20-25B in capex on $3-3.4B guided revenue.

results.title: Hyperscalers Outsource $12B Compute as Power Grids Tighten; Neocloud Model Validated · Slicast
highlights:
OpenAI's $12 billion CoreWeave deal and Nscale's $103.4 billion IPO contracts validate hyperscaler outsourcing of compute to specialized neoclouds, but power infrastructure emerges as the binding constraint on the $1 trillion capex cycle.

Hyperscalers are outsourcing GPU compute capacity at scale. OpenAI committed $12 billion to CoreWeave for inference infrastructure; Anthropic committed $11.6 billion to Akamai. Nscale's IPO filing disclosed $103.4 billion in contracted AI infrastructure demand—the highest visibility yet into committed neocloud capacity. CoreWeave alone signed $250 billion in new customer commitments in Q3. The economic logic is clear: building and operating GPU clusters costs more capital than paying a specialized neocloud to do it. Neoclouds have lower capex intensity per unit and absorb margin pressure hyperscalers cannot.

Pricing power is inverting in neoclouds' favor after two years of deflation. H100 rental rates bottomed at $3.38 per hour in 2026, but Nebius announced price increases of 17–21 percent across its lineup, effective October 1. The move signals supply tightening—the first material recovery since 2024. Nscale's IPO at ~$35 billion valuation despite ~$1 billion cumulative losses proves investor appetite for contracted demand. That pricing power is real and tightening.

Power infrastructure has become the binding constraint. Oracle invoked force majeure on Project Jupiter due to grid delays, stalling an $18 billion construction loan. The federal government responded with $1.9 billion in grid investment to unlock 23 gigawatts of data-center capacity. But OpenAI forecasts $856 billion in compute spending through 2030. Twenty-three gigawatts is a down payment, not a solution. Grid delays are now the primary bottleneck to hyperscaler capex, not capital or chip availability.

results.title: Locking in compute: why long-tenor, prepaid GPU contracts work, and when they stop | GPU Capital
highlights:
- A long-tenor contract with a prepayment is a trade: the customer buys reserved capacity and a locked price; the neocloud and its capital partner buy contracted cash flow and less capital at risk.
- In September 2026 a multi-year B300 commitment priced at roughly 50 to 60% of the on-demand rate.
- In our illustration, moving from a two-year to a five-year term cuts the rate by 18% while the owner’s capital at risk falls from 73% to 44% of the node’s cost.
- The trade stops working when expectations diverge: when customers expect rates to fall or hardware to age out, or providers expect rates to rise.

...

A long-tenor GPU contract with a customer prepayment is a trade, not a concession. The customer buys reserved capacity and a locked price. The neocloud and its capital partner buy contracted cash flow and less capital at risk. In 2026 that trade is working because both sides fear the same thing: scarcity.

It stops working when expectations diverge. If customers believe rates will fall, or hardware will be obsolete before the contract ends, they stop committing. If providers believe rates will rise, they stop offering long terms at fixed prices. The skill is knowing which side of that line the market is on, deal by deal.

## The 2026 backdrop: a steep tenor curve and rising capex

B300 shows how steeply the market prices commitment. The same GPU rents for roughly $7.90 an hour on demand and about $4 to $5 an hour on a multi-year contract. That gap is the price of certainty, and scarcity sets it.

Meanwhile the cost of building new capacity is rising. Memory is the driver, and it shows up directly in server quotes.

results.title: When GPU Contracts Break · CCIR
highlights:
## The record, 38 cases, 2022 to 2026

- Most fleets were re-let in place, and the GPUs stayed in their racks. The exception was a sale: WhiteFiber's 126 H200 servers.
- When the GPUs were leased to new customers, revenue per installed GPU-hour settled at about 50% to 70% of the earlier rate. Most earlier rates were set in 2023 and 2024, when H100 rental rates were higher.
- Time to re-let ran from under a month to about three quarters, longer for larger fleets.
- No lender- or court-forced GPU sale is on record. No GPU fleet went through a UCC foreclosure, a bankruptcy sale or a receivership.
- One filed equipment price: WhiteFiber sold 126 H200 servers in early 2026 for $207,000 each. That is about $25,900 per GPU, about 90% of the order price (case). Our current H200 market value is $30,900 per GPU, all-in (/hardware).
- Stress case on today's values, after 3 to 12 months with no rent and a new contract at 65% of the recent rate:

| System | Value kept | Stress value, midpoint | Months with no rent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B300 HGX per GPU | 45% to 55% | $41.8k | 3.8 to 12 |
| B200 HGX per GPU | 43% to 57% | $26.6k | 3.9 to 12 |
| H200 HGX per GPU | 42% to 64% | $16.4k | 3.4 to 11.4 |
| H100 HGX per GPU | 28% to 50% | $6.9k | 3.0 to 9.3 |
| GB300 / GB200 NVL72 per rack | about 41% | $2.70M / $1.70M | 12 |

...

When a big customer leaves, the fleet usually stays in place. Two owners in our cases first rented theirs on demand, to many smaller customers. By October 2025, Northern Data said it was moving those spot buyers onto reserved contracts. With demand for GPU time strong, re-letting can sound quick. The steps below walk through what it takes in practice.

1. Prepare the machines. The old customer's data and software are still on the servers. The owner erases the local drives to a federal standard, NIST SP 800-88. It checks the firmware, the low-level code under the operating system, so the next customer can trust it. It reinstalls the operating system and drivers. It changes the network settings so each new customer is walled off from the others. Then it runs every GPU under full load to catch failing parts before anyone pays. We estimate two to four weeks with no rent, while power and site costs keep running. At scale it can run longer. One large GPU cloud's IPO filing says that in a badly set-up cloud, "GPU acceptance, provisioning, burn-in and testing issues can take months."
2. Change how the fleet is sold. Under a big contract, one customer takes the whole cluster for years. It often runs its own software on top and deals with the owner through one account team. On-demand service works differently. Many customers rent a few servers each, by the hour, and come and go. The owner needs software that hands out servers, bills by the hour and keeps each customer's data and traffic apart. It also needs support for many small accounts. A fleet built for one customer may have none of this. One owner in our cases moved two clusters from reserved contracts to on-demand service between December 2024 and February 2025. Its cloud revenue fell $9.9 million in a quarter. It said: "We encountered technical issues in moving the capacity which have since been resolved" (case). Another GPU cloud's IPO filing warns that its halls may not suit replacement customers "without meaningful retrofitting or upgrading."
3. Fill it a block at a time. A big customer takes thousands of GPUs in one deal. On-demand customers rent a few servers each. Most GPU clouds we checked post prices for a few hundred GPUs at most and quote larger blocks on request. So a large fleet needs many customers to fill. Each one must be checked before it can rent. U.S. export guidance asks sellers of advanced chips to check who their customers are and who those customers serve. One owner with about 22,000 GPUs began rebuilding for on-demand access at the end of March 2025. Utilization was 11% in August, 62% in December and about 85% in March 2026 (case).

...

1. Default. The tenant stops paying today. The servers or racks stay in place.
2. Time with no rent. The owner wipes and re-certifies the systems, finds tenants and runs acceptance tests. A larger fleet takes longer, and so does a system that few operators rent. We start at 3 months for 1,000 H100s. The time scales up with fleet size and down with the number of operators, from 3 to 12 months.
3. New contract. The owner signs for the same term as recent contracts, at 65% of the recent contract rate. When the GPUs were leased to new customers, revenue per installed GPU-hour settled at about 50% to 70% of the earlier level.
4. After it. The unit re-leases at published interruptible rates at 70% utilization, falling with age, until rent stops covering costs.

results.title: Good news for AI bubble skeptics. The era of being able to short GPU rental prices is finally coming.｜会社員薬剤師の投資判断ノート
highlights:
I saw the news that Nebius is raising its on-demand GPU rental rates again starting October 1st. This applies to select NVIDIA chips, with increases ranging from 17% to 21%. This is the second price hike in three months.

In discussions about the AI bubble, you often see claims that "GPUs will eventually be in surplus," "the value of older generation GPUs will drop," and "massive depreciation will become a problem." If that's the case, we should just look at the actual prices.

How much are H100s, H200s, and B200s being rented for right now, and are prices rising or falling? I thought that if I could check this as easily as checking stock prices, I could directly observe the supply and demand in the AI compute resource market.

...

What I especially want to see is the H100. If H100 prices hold steady even as new GPUs appear one after another, it means there is still sufficient demand for older generation compute resources. Conversely, if prices for the H100 start to collapse, it will be an interesting signal for considering the residual value of GPUs and the profitability of neo-clouds.

However, the prices seen here are not "someone's contract unit price." They are figures based on publicly available on-demand rental quotes, standardized by generation. Even for the same H100, there is a large spread depending on the provider. I believe the index is meant to look at the center of the market.

...

CME Group is partnering with Silicon Data to prepare futures linked to H100 and B200 GPU rental prices. The product names are Silicon Data H100 Rental Index Futures and Silicon Data B200 Rental Index Futures. The codes are GPU1 and GPU2. Settlement is in cash, and the contract unit is 730 GPU-hours, which is the computing power of renting one GPU for one month.

The target is not the GPU itself. It is the price of renting the GPU's computing power. Even in the CME's explanation, the content of the index is stated to be the on-demand hourly rate of Neoclouds, not hyperscalers.

The initial plan was for a listing on October 5, 2026. In other words, as of the time of writing this article (end of September 2026), it has not yet been officially listed. It is reported that the CFTC has extended its review and will not make the October 5th deadline. The regulators' reasoning was that the spot market for compute resources is fragmented and opaque.

results.title: Blog | Neptune Infotech
highlights:
## Why GPU Rental Prices Vary Across Clouds

Several factors drive the price gaps:

- Supply chain dynamics: Recent memory shortages have pushed B200 and H200 prices higher.
- Provider pricing models: Hyperscalers, niche neoclouds, and serverless platforms each apply different markup strategies.
- Geographic location and egress costs: Data‑transfer fees can add hidden expenses.
- Demand spikes: Prices can surge during AI research conferences or model‑training marathons.

## Current September 2026 Spot Prices for Popular GPUs

Our FastGPU monitor captured live rates on 27 September 2026 at 04:11 UTC. The same GPU can cost several times more depending on the marketplace.

- The NVIDIA H100 fell to $3.38 per hour on several spot markets, according to Shattered.io.
- Earlier in the year, pricing data showed H100 instances as low as $2.01 per hour (May 2026).
- While exact RTX 4090 numbers fluctuate, many providers list rates between $2.50 – $4.00 per hour, often changing within minutes.
- B200 and H200 GPUs command a premium, reflecting the ongoing memory supply crunch.

...

Analysts expect pricing to remain volatile as new GPU generations (e.g., H200) enter the market and memory shortages persist. Competition among niche neoclouds may drive down rates, but hyperscalers could leverage scale to offer bundled discounts for larger workloads.

results.title: Nscale's $103B backlog is mostly IOU: a playbook to price any AI-cloud IPO | AInvest
highlights:
- Nscale, a London-based AI cloud provider backed by Nvidia

...

- However, only $2.6B of the backlog is "active" (generating revenue), with 95% of 461,000 contracted GPUs undelivered, and H1 2026 revenue at just $140.6M (0.4% of backlog).

- The backlog relies heavily on two clients (Microsoft and Anthropic, 85% of total value), with Anthropic’s $44.6B deal contingent on unsecured West Virginia infrastructure and financing.

...

The first test is the recognition rate - how much of the contracted value ever becomes recognized revenue. The two numbers are not the same. On Nscale's own table, only $2.6 billion of that $103.4 billion is "active" - signed contracts whose terms have begun and are generating revenue. The rest is contracted but not yet delivered. Nscale recognizes revenue under long-term take-or-pay contracts whose terms commence only upon successful delivery of GPU clusters, so the gap GAP-- is not cosmetic: of roughly 461,000 active-or-contracted GPUs, only about 25,000, roughly 5%, are live.

...

Fourth, counterparty-financing. A cloud must lay out the capex years before it can recognize a dollar of that take-or-pay revenue. Nscale has disclosed it has not obtained binding commitments for the financing required to perform the Anthropic agreements, and it carries roughly $29 billion of outstanding commitments - equipment, construction, leases - against a $35 billion target valuation, with no long-term supplier contracts that lock GPU supply or pricing. The revenue it shows today is largely supported by customer prepayments carried as $6.5 billion of deferred revenue.
